name: East Sikkim
tagline: Gangtok, the high lakes and the old Silk Route
summary: East Sikkim is the part of Sikkim around Gangtok, the state capital, running up to Tsomgo Lake and the Nathu La border pass and down through the farm villages of Aritar and the Silk Route to Zuluk. Go for monasteries, high lakes and mountain roads; October to December and March to May are the best months.
meta_description: East Sikkim travel guide: Gangtok, Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La, Zuluk and Aritar. Permits, best months, costs per day, how to get there and honest tips.
intro: East Sikkim is the most visited part of the state and the easiest to reach. Gangtok, the capital, sits on a ridge at about 1,650 m, about 114 km from Siliguri, and most journeys into Sikkim start here. From the town, roads climb east to Tsomgo Lake at 3,753 m and Nathu La at 4,310 m on the border with Tibet, and south-east to the farming villages and old trade route around Rongli and Zuluk.

In 2021 the old East Sikkim district was split into Gangtok district and the new Pakyong district. Travellers still use the old name for the whole area, and so do we. Gangtok, Rumtek, Tsomgo and Nathu La lie in Gangtok district; Aritar, Rongli and Zuluk lie in Pakyong district, along with Pakyong airport.

The region packs a lot into a short distance. In a single day you can go from subtropical valleys where oranges and cardamom grow to bare, snow-covered ridges above 4,000 m. That makes it rewarding but also demanding: altitude, weather and permits all shape what you can do, and plans need some slack.

Most visitors spend three or four nights in Gangtok with day trips to Tsomgo, Nathu La and Rumtek. With five or six nights you can add the Silk Route through Aritar and Zuluk, which feels quieter and more rural. East Sikkim also links easily with Kalimpong and Darjeeling to the south and with North Sikkim to the north.

highlights.title: Gangtok and MG Marg
highlights.text: A clean, walkable capital with monasteries, viewpoints and good food, and the base for most trips.

highlights.title: Tsomgo Lake
highlights.text: A glacial lake at 3,753 m, frozen in midwinter and ringed by rhododendrons in spring.

highlights.title: Nathu La
highlights.text: The border pass at 4,310 m on the old road to Lhasa, open to Indian nationals with a permit.

highlights.title: Rumtek Monastery
highlights.text: The largest monastery in Sikkim and the seat in exile of the 16th Karmapa.

highlights.title: The Silk Route through Zuluk
highlights.text: Hairpin roads, sunrise over Kangchenjunga from Thambi and quiet homestays at about 3,000 m.

highlights.title: Aritar and Lampokhari
highlights.text: A gentle farm village with a long forest lake, a good first or last night on the Silk Route.

people: East Sikkim is home to Nepali-speaking communities, who form the majority, including Rai, Limbu, Gurung, Tamang, Sherpa, Newar, Chhetri and Bahun families, alongside the Bhutia and Lepcha peoples whose ancestors shaped the old kingdom. Buddhism and Hinduism are both widely practised, often side by side, and many villages also keep older nature and ancestor traditions. Gangtok has long-settled Tibetan, Marwari and Bihari trading families too. Nepali is the common language of the street, and English is widely understood in Gangtok. People are courteous and reserved; a greeting, a little patience and respect at monasteries and homes go a long way.

budget_day.covers: per person per day: a guesthouse or homestay twin room shared, local meals, shared jeeps and a share of a pooled permit vehicle
per person per day: a good mid-range hotel, meals in decent restaurants, and a private car shared between two for sightseeing and permit days
per person per day: heritage or resort rooms, most meals in the hotel, a private SUV with driver throughout and a guide for monastery visits

months.weather: Cold and clear, about 0–12°C in Gangtok
months.summary: Gangtok is cold but often sunny, with good mountain views. Tsomgo is usually frozen and snow can close the road to Nathu La and above Zuluk for days.
months.tip: Keep a spare day in Gangtok for the Tsomgo trip in case snow closes the road.

months.weather: Cold, clear spells, about 2–14°C in Gangtok
months.summary: Still winter at height, with frozen lakes and snow on the passes. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, brings ceremonies at Rumtek and other monasteries.
months.tip: Check Losar dates, as some shops close for the first days of the new year.

months.weather: Mild days, cold nights, about 6–18°C in Gangtok
months.summary: Spring begins, with rhododendrons flowering lower down and snow still lining the road to Nathu La. A good month for snow with a better chance of open roads.
months.tip: Pack for both mild days in Gangtok and freezing wind at Nathu La.

months.summary: One of the best months. Rhododendrons flower on the way to Tsomgo, roads are usually open and the Silk Route is green and clear in the mornings.
months.tip: Start early on permit days; spring haze and cloud build after midday.

months.summary: Peak season for Indian families, with crowds at Tsomgo and full hotels in Gangtok. Flowers carpet the slopes around the high lakes.
months.tip: Book hotels and cars well ahead, especially around school holidays.

months.summary: The monsoon begins mid-month. Early June can still be good, but cloud, rain and landslides increase as the month goes on.
months.tip: Allow extra hours on NH10 and keep plans flexible after heavy rain.

months.summary: The wettest time. Mountains are hidden, landslides close roads and permit trips are often cancelled. Gangtok itself is green and quiet.
months.tip: Only travel if you are flexible, and buy travel insurance that covers delays.

months.summary: Still monsoon, with frequent rain and road disruption. Pang Lhabsol may fall in late August, with masked dances in Gangtok.
months.tip: Check the Pang Lhabsol date; if it falls in your stay, it is worth timing a visit around it.

months.summary: The monsoon fades late in the month and the hills are at their greenest. Pang Lhabsol often falls in September.
months.tip: Late September can be a good-value window before October prices rise.

months.weather: Clear and fresh, about 11–20°C in Gangtok
months.summary: The best views of the year begin, with blue skies over Kangchenjunga and open roads. It is also peak season, especially around the Durga Puja holidays.
months.tip: Book early for the Puja holidays, when Bengal travellers fill hotels and cars.

months.weather: Cool and very clear, about 7–17°C in Gangtok
months.summary: Excellent visibility and fewer crowds than October. Nights are cold at Zuluk and the high road over Nathang may see early snow.
months.tip: Go to Thambi viewpoint for sunrise; November skies are usually the clearest.

months.weather: Cold and clear, about 3–14°C in Gangtok
months.summary: Clear, cold days and the first heavy snows higher up. Losoong and the Kagyed Chaam bring masked dances to Gangtok before the Christmas rush.
months.tip: Carry warm layers and book the Christmas week early.

getting_there: The nearest airport is Bagdogra (IXB) near Siliguri, about 124 km and 4.5–5 hours by road from Gangtok. New Jalpaiguri (NJP) is the main railway station, about 120 km away. Pakyong airport, about 30 km from Gangtok, has had irregular commercial flights; check current status before you travel. From Siliguri, NH10 follows the Teesta river through Sevoke and Rangpo to Gangtok in 4–5 hours by reserved car (₹3,500–5,000) or 4.5–5.5 hours by shared jeep (₹350–450 a seat). Landslides close NH10 several times a year, especially in the monsoon, when cars detour via Kalimpong and Pedong or Algarah, adding 1–3 hours. For Aritar and Zuluk, turn off at Rangpo towards Rorathang, Rhenock and Rongli.
permits: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Gangtok, Rumtek or Aritar. They need permits arranged through a registered travel agent for Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La (Nathu La permits a day ahead, and the pass is usually closed to tourists on Mondays and Tuesdays), and a Protected Area Permit for Zuluk and the Silk Route, issued at Rongli. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Inner Line Permit, formally a Restricted Area Permit, to enter Sikkim; it is free and issued at Rangpo, Bagdogra airport, Sikkim House in Delhi and the Sikkim Tourism office in Siliguri. Foreigners can visit Tsomgo Lake on a day trip with a Protected Area Permit in a group of two or more, but cannot go to Nathu La or Zuluk. Rules and fees are indicative. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Four to six days covers the region well. Three or four nights in Gangtok allow a day each for the town, Tsomgo with Nathu La, and Rumtek, plus a spare day for weather. Add two or three nights for the Silk Route through Aritar and Zuluk if you want a quieter, more rural side.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit East Sikkim?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest skies and mountain views, and March to May brings flowers and milder weather. January and February are cold, with frozen lakes and occasional road closures from snow. June to September is the monsoon, with rain, cloud and landslides that disrupt trips to Tsomgo, Nathu La and Zuluk.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for Gangtok, Rumtek or Aritar, but need permits through a registered agent for Tsomgo, Nathu La and Zuluk. Foreigners need the Sikkim Inner Line Permit to enter the state, can visit Tsomgo with an extra permit, and cannot go to Nathu La or Zuluk. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get to Gangtok from Bagdogra or NJP?
faqs.a: By reserved car, the 120–124 km drive takes about 4–5 hours and costs ₹3,500–5,500 depending on the vehicle. Shared jeeps leave from Siliguri near the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus and from NJP station for about ₹350–450 a seat. SNT buses are slower and cheaper. Allow extra time in the monsoon.

faqs.q: Is East Sikkim good for a first trip to the Himalaya?
faqs.a: Yes. Gangtok is comfortable and well connected, and the high places are reachable as day trips rather than overnight stays at altitude, which suits first-timers. Spend at least one night in Gangtok before going to Tsomgo or Nathu La, and keep a spare day for weather and permit cancellations.

faqs.q: What is the Silk Route in East Sikkim?
faqs.a: It is the name used by travel agents for the old trade route from Kalimpong to Lhasa through Rhenock, Rongli, Zuluk, Gnathang and Jelep La. Today it is a two to four night road trip with homestays at Aritar and Zuluk, the zigzag road and Thambi viewpoint. Only Indian nationals can get the permit beyond Rongli.

faqs.q: How much does a trip to East Sikkim cost?
faqs.a: A budget traveller can manage on ₹1,800–2,500 a day using guesthouses, local food and shared vehicles. A Value trip with good hotels and a private car costs about ₹4,000–6,000 per person a day, and Comfort ₹8,000–14,000. Permit-day vehicles are the biggest variable, so share them where you can.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a concern in East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Gangtok at about 1,650 m causes no problems, but Tsomgo at 3,753 m, Nathu La at 4,310 m and the high road above Zuluk at about 4,000 m can cause headaches and breathlessness. Spend a night in Gangtok or Aritar first, climb slowly, drink water and descend if symptoms worsen.

faqs.q: Can I combine East Sikkim with Darjeeling or North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes. Kalimpong is about 3 hours from Gangtok and Darjeeling about 4 hours, making an easy combined loop from Siliguri. North Sikkim permits for Lachung and Lachen are arranged in Gangtok, so many trips do Gangtok, then North Sikkim, then return through Gangtok. Allow at least eight nights for a combined trip.
